chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Abu Talib Abdullah ibn al-Salt, who said:

Al-Khalil ibn Hashim wrote to Zil al-Ri'asatayn (the one with two governorships), who was the governor of Naysabur, that a man from the Magians had died and bequeathed something of his wealth to the poor. So the judge of Naysabur took it and placed it among the poor Muslims. So Al-Khalil wrote to Zil al-Ri'asatayn about that. So he asked Al-Ma'mun about it, and he said, 'I have nothing regarding it.' So he asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), and Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: 'The Magian did not bequeath to the poor Muslims, but it is fitting that the amount of that wealth be taken from the charity funds (sadaqah) and returned to the poor Magians.'

key_terms.أَبُو الْحَسَنِ: Abu al-Hasan (Imam al-Rida, peace be upon him)
key_terms.ذِي الرِّئَاسَتَيْنِ: One with two governorships (a title for the governor of Naysabur)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a Magian's bequest to the poor in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi illustrates the Shia juristic principle of respecting the specific intent (niyyah) of a non-Muslim testator when bequeathing to 'the poor,' distinguishing it from the general Islamic concept of sadaqah. Imam al-Rida (AS) prescribes deducting the equivalent amount from the public treasury to pay the Magian poor, thereby ensuring the bequest is fulfilled without conflating the two distinct groups. This ruling highlights the practical application of justice and contractual fidelity in inter-community financial transactions during the Abbasid era.
